items.headline: AST SpaceMobile signs $1.3B engine deal with Firefly for 20‑ton Blacklift rocket
items.title: AST SpaceMobile unveils $1.3 billion engine deal with Firefly Aerospace to power new heavy-lift rocket
items.scifi_hook: A new heavy‑lift rocket will lift a fleet of orbiting cellular towers into space.
items.eli5: AST will use Firefly’s engine to build a 20‑ton rocket that can launch five broadband satellites at once.
items.why: It gives the company independent launch access and expands global connectivity.
items.text: An artist’s rendering of AST SpaceMobile’s proposed new rocket, Blacklift. Graphic: AST SpaceMobile Texas-based companies AST SpaceMobile and Firefly Aerospace announced a $1.3 billion agreement to license a rocket engine that will power a new, heavy-lift rocket starting in 2028, if all goes to plan. The proposed launcher is called Blacklift and AST SpaceMobile classifies it as a 20-ton rocket, which would put it in the same category of SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan. Following the trend of SpaceX using its Falcon 9 rockets principally to launch its Starlink satellites, AST SpaceMobile will focus its launch capacity to fly its BlueBird satellites to orbit. The company said the rocket will be capable of launching five of its BlueBird satellites at a time. “The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market, providing AST SpaceMobile with regular unconstrained access to orbit and providing for most favorable owners’ economics in the industry,” said Abel Avellan, Founder, Chairman, and CEO of AST SpaceMobile. “This will accelerate our mission to build a new layer of global connectivity, extending connectivity beyond terrestrial networks and helping to bring AI-enabled services wherever people live, work and travel.” Few details about the rocket itself were released alongside the announcement on Friday. items.title: Pakistani astronaut to board Shenzhou 24 and become the first foreigner on China's space station
items.scifi_hook: A Pakistani pilot will float aboard China’s Shenzhou 24, marking the first non‑Chinese visitor.

items.headline: Canadian Uranium eyes growth as it files Rook II exploration report
items.title: Canadian Uranium eyes acquisitions as Rook II exploration takes shape
items.scifi_hook: Canada’s uranium explorer maps new deposits to help power a low‑carbon future.
items.eli5: The company reported 28 uranium spots in Saskatchewan, aiming to boost Canada’s uranium output.
items.why: Expanding uranium supply supports global clean‑energy and nuclear power expansion.
items.text: As Canada joins the race racing to secure reliable, low-carbon power as part of its first-ever national Nuclear Energy Strategy, released in June , and technology giants’ growing investment in nuclear power are sharpening the focus on the fuel behind that expansion: uranium. Canada has the resources and project pipeline needed to achieve the federal government’s goal of doubling uranium exports by 2035, but success will hinge on exploration, and project execution. For Canadian Uranium (CSE: CANU) advisor Arni Johannson, the search leads back to Saskatchewan. The veteran uranium investor founded Titan Uranium, which staked and funded early exploration at Rook I, the property now home to NexGen Energy’s (TSX, NYSE: NXE; ASX: NXG) Arrow deposit. NexGen began construction this summer of its Rook uranium mine in northern Saskatchewan, the largest development-stage uranium deposit in Canada, with a C$2.2 billion capex build plan.
